cloze.text: The maximum accumulated (lifetime) dose for a radiation worker = {{c1::the worker's age × 10 mSv}}.
Radiolucent areas appear {{c1::dark}} on a radiograph; they are produced by {{c2::less dense}} structures that readily permit the passage of X-rays.
cloze.extra: e.g., cysts look darker because they contain no dense material.

cloze.text: Radiopaque areas appear {{c1::light}} on a radiograph; they are produced by {{c2::denser}} structures that absorbed the radiation so it did not reach the receptor.
The {{c1::lamina dura}} — the dense bone around the roots — is an example of a radiopaque structure.
Beam intensity is affected by {{c1::mA}}, {{c2::kVp}}, {{c3::distance}}, and {{c4::exposure time}}.
To increase beam intensity: {{c1::increase}} mA, kVp and time, and {{c2::decrease}} the distance.
To decrease beam intensity: {{c1::decrease}} mA, kVp and time, and {{c2::increase}} the distance.
Aluminum filters remove the {{c1::less penetrating, longer}} wavelengths from the X-ray beam.
Radiographic density is also called the {{c1::darkness}} of the image.
Density (darkness) is directly proportional to {{c1::milliamperage (mA)}}, {{c2::kVp}}, and {{c3::exposure time}}.
To maintain similar density: if exposure time is increased, milliamperage must be {{c1::decreased}}; if time is decreased, mA must be {{c2::increased}}.
Density is {{c1::decreased}} (the image is lighter) if the target structure is dense.
Radiographic contrast is dependent on {{c1::kVp}}.
Increased kVp produces many shades of gray = {{c1::long-scale, low}} contrast — best for detecting {{c2::bone abnormalities, changes in bone density and periodontitis progression}}.
Decreased kVp produces more black-and-white areas = {{c1::short-scale, high}} contrast — best for detecting {{c2::caries}}.

Sharpness increases when the focal spot (tungsten target of the anode) is {{c1::small}}, the object-to-receptor distance is {{c2::short}}, and the tube (target/source)-to-receptor distance is {{c3::long}}.
{{c1::Patient and tube head movement}} are the most common reasons for a fuzzy (unsharp) image.
Increasing the tube (target)-to-receptor distance gives {{c1::more parallel}} rays and therefore {{c2::less}} magnification.
A {{c1::shorter}} object-to-receptor distance produces less magnification.
In the paralleling technique the receptor and the long axis of the tooth are {{c1::parallel}} to each other, and the central ray is directed {{c2::perpendicular}} to both — to prevent distortion.
A periapical (PA) image captures the {{c1::crown, CEJ, root, apex and surrounding bone}}.
cloze.extra: Main uses: diagnosis of periodontal disease, pathology, endodontic therapy and implants.

cloze.text: A bitewing (BW) captures the {{c1::crowns, contacts and height of the alveolar bone}}; its main use is diagnosing {{c2::interproximal caries}}.
A vertical bitewing is like a bitewing but includes more of the {{c1::bone level}}; it is used for detecting {{c2::early periodontal disease}}.
An occlusal image captures the bone around the teeth, floor of the mouth, {{c1::sialoliths}} and {{c2::supernumerary teeth}}; it is useful when the patient has {{c3::limited jaw opening}}.
A full-mouth series (FMX/CMS) images the entire dentition using a combination of {{c1::PAs and BWs}}, for comprehensive dental assessment.
The bisecting technique is based on the {{c1::rule of isometry}}.
In the bisecting technique, the angle formed by the {{c1::receptor and the long axis of the tooth}} is bisected, and the central beam is directed at {{c2::90°}} to the bisecting line.
The paralleling technique is also called the {{c1::long-cone}} technique.
The paralleling technique requires a {{c1::receptor holder}}, which positions the receptor {{c2::farther from}} the tooth surface.

Paralleling gives a more accurate image with less distortion than bisecting; the increased receptor-to-tooth distance can cause {{c1::magnification}}, compensated for by an increased {{c2::tube-to-tooth}} distance.
Mandibular (topographic) occlusal technique: the head is tilted {{c1::backward}} and the central ray is directed {{c2::through the chin}}.
Maxillary (topographic) occlusal technique: the occlusal plane is {{c1::parallel to the floor}} and the central ray is directed through the {{c2::tip of the nose}}.

Cross-sectional maxillary occlusal technique: the occlusal plane is parallel to the floor, the beam is {{c1::perpendicular to the receptor}}, and the central ray is directed {{c2::between the eyebrows}}.

Cross-sectional mandibular occlusal technique: the head is tilted back until the {{c1::ala-tragus}} line is almost {{c2::perpendicular}} to the floor; the beam is perpendicular to the receptor and directed {{c3::inferior to the chin}}.

The buccal object rule shows whether an object is {{c1::buccal or lingual}}; a single PA or BW shows only its {{c2::anteroposterior}} location, because a radiograph is a two-dimensional image of a three-dimensional space.
The buccal object rule needs {{c1::two}} images (PA or BW), the second taken from a different {{c2::horizontal or vertical}} angle.
SLOB: if the tube head and the object move in the {{c1::same}} direction, the object is {{c2::lingual}}; if they move in {{c3::opposite}} directions, the object is {{c4::buccal}}.
cloze.extra: SLOB = Same Lingual, Opposite Buccal. Compare the two images: does the object move with or against the tube-head shift?

cloze.text: Overlap (overlapping contacts) is caused by incorrect {{c1::horizontal}} angulation; correct it by directing the beam {{c2::through the contacts}}.
Foreshortening (teeth too short) is caused by {{c1::too much}} vertical angulation; correct by {{c2::decreasing}} the angulation.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: the tooth is a building — if it looks too short you are looking at it from high above → angulation too much → decrease it.

cloze.text: Elongation (teeth too long) is caused by {{c1::too little}} vertical angulation; correct by {{c2::increasing}} the vertical angulation.
A cone cut happens when the {{c1::PID}} does not cover the entire sensor; the PID should cover the entire surface of the receptor.
A double exposure results from taking {{c1::multiple images on the same receptor}}; prevent it by {{c2::clearing phosphor plates}} before reusing them.
cloze.extra: The book says "same film"; the exam no longer uses film terminology — the idea applies to any receptor, e.g. PSP plates.

cloze.text: Panoramic images are useful for evaluating {{c1::impacted teeth}}, {{c2::eruption patterns}}, and {{c3::TMJ problems}}.
Panoramic images are usually not clear and detailed enough to assess {{c1::caries and periodontal disease}}.
On a panoramic image, objects {{c1::inside}} the focal trough are clear, whereas objects {{c2::outside}} it are blurred.
A cephalometric projection provides a {{c1::lateral view of the skull}} and evaluates {{c2::trauma and facial growth}}.
A lateral jaw exposure evaluates the {{c1::posterior portion of the mandible}} or lateral areas too large for periapical receptors.
cloze.extra: Useful for areas that cannot be adequately captured with standard intraoral techniques.

cloze.text: The {{c1::Water's}} projection is specifically designed to visualize the {{c2::maxillary sinuses}}.
MRI uses {{c1::magnetic fields and radio waves}} and is particularly good for {{c2::soft tissue}} contrast, e.g. imaging the {{c3::TMJ}}.

CT/CBCT provides a {{c1::3D}}, cross-sectional image with detailed bone and soft-tissue information; it is used for {{c2::implant planning}} and soft-tissue lesions, especially in the {{c3::salivary glands}}.
{{c1::CBCT (cone beam CT)}} is the form of CT specifically designed for dental and maxillofacial imaging.
Sialography involves injecting a {{c1::contrast medium}} into the salivary ducts; it detects {{c2::salivary stones and other blockages}}.

typein.question: MPD for a non-occupationally exposed person (general public) — in mSv per year?

mcq.question: A 35-year-old dental hygienist asks what her maximum accumulated lifetime radiation dose is. Which is correct?
mcq.explanation: Maximum accumulated dose = age × 10 mSv → 35 × 10 = 350 mSv. 50 mSv is the annual occupational MPD, not the lifetime total; 500 mSv would be for a 50-year-old.

mcq.question: A clinician switches from a 16-inch PID to an 8-inch PID without changing exposure settings. What happens to beam intensity at the skin?
mcq.explanation: Inverse square law: distance halved → factor 2, squared = 4; distance DECREASED so do not invert → 4× the intensity. 'Reduced to 1/4' is the answer for going from 8 to 16 inches.

mcq.question: Which change would produce the SHARPEST image with the least penumbra?
mcq.explanation: A long tube-to-receptor distance (with a small focal spot and short object–receptor distance) gives the least penumbra. A larger focal spot and longer object–receptor distance both increase blurring.

mcq.question: Which statement correctly compares the paralleling and bisecting techniques?
options: A. Paralleling places the receptor close to the tooth and uses a short PID
B. Bisecting aims the central ray perpendicular to the long axis of the tooth
C. Paralleling produces less distortion; its magnification is offset by a longer tube-to-tooth distance
D. Bisecting is less affected by the shape of the palate
mcq.answer: C. Paralleling produces less distortion; its magnification is offset by a longer tube-to-tooth distance
mcq.explanation: Paralleling = receptor parallel to the tooth, beam 90° to both, receptor held farther from the tooth, magnification compensated by longer tube distance. Bisecting aims at 90° to the bisecting line (not the long axis) and is more distorted because of the palate.

mcq.question: A molar PA shows a radiopaque object near the apex. For a second PA the tube head is shifted mesially, and the object appears to move distally relative to the teeth. Where is the object?
options: C. In the same plane as the teeth
D. Cannot be determined without a third image
mcq.explanation: Tube head mesial, object distal = opposite directions → Opposite = Buccal (SLOB). Lingual would require the object to move in the same direction as the tube head.

mcq.question: On a maxillary canine PA, the canine looks abnormally long. Which correction should the hygienist make on the retake?
options: C. Change the horizontal angulation to pass through the contacts
D. Reposition the PID to cover the entire sensor
mcq.explanation: An elongated image = too little vertical angulation → increase it. Decreasing vertical angulation corrects foreshortening (tooth too short); horizontal angulation corrects overlap.

mcq.question: A patient reports swelling under the jaw at mealtimes. The dentist wants to visualize the structure of the salivary ducts and locate an obstruction. Which technique is designed for this?
mcq.explanation: Sialography injects contrast medium into the salivary ducts to show their structure and any stones/blockages. Water's shows the maxillary sinuses; cephalometric is a lateral skull view for growth/trauma.

mcq.question: Which imaging modality does NOT use X-rays and is best for soft-tissue contrast of the TMJ?
mcq.explanation: MRI uses magnetic fields and radio waves and excels at soft-tissue contrast (e.g. TMJ disc). CBCT gives 3D images but uses X-rays.
